definition: Computational humor is a branch of computational linguistics and artificial intelligence which uses computers in humor research.
details: It is a relatively new area, with the first dedicated conference organized in 1996. The first "computer model of a sense of humor" was suggested by Suslov as early as 1992. Investigation of the general scheme of the information processing show a possibility of a specific malfunction, conditioned by the necessity of a quick deletion from consciousness of a false version. This specific malfunction can be identified with a humorous effect on the psychological grounds; however, an essentially new ingredient, a role of timing, is added to a well known role of ambiguity. In biological systems, a sense of humour inevitably develops in the course of evolution, because its biological function consists in quickening the transmission of processed information into consciousness and in a more effective use of brain resources. A realization of this algorithm in neural networks explains naturally the mechanism of laughter: deletion of a false version corresponds to zeroing of some part of the neural network and excessive energy of neurons is thrown out to the motor cortex, arousing muscular contractions. Unfortunately, a practical realization of this algorithm needs extensive databases, whose creation in the automatic regime was suggested only recently . As a result, this magistral direction was not developed properly and subsequent investigations (see below) accepted somewhat specialized colouring.

explainer.lead: Computational humor uses computers to investigate how humor arises and how it might be modeled. It connects a familiar human experience with questions about language, timing, information processing, and neural networks.

tiers.eli5: Imagine thinking a sentence means one thing, then suddenly realizing you got it wrong and quickly switching to the right meaning. That surprise can feel funny, like expecting a ball to roll one way and seeing it bounce another. Computational humor studies this kind of experience with computers.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer can approach humor as an information-processing problem involving ambiguity, a false interpretation, and the timing of its correction. Suslov's proposed neural-network implementation associates deletion of the false version with zeroing part of a network. A major practical obstacle was the need for extensive databases, whose automatic creation was suggested only later.
tiers.paperLevel: Computational humor is a branch of computational linguistics and artificial intelligence that uses computers in humor research. Suslov's 1992 model can be summarized as: ambiguous input -> false version -> rapid deletion from consciousness -> humorous effect, with timing complementing ambiguity. Its proposed neural realization maps deletion to zeroing part of a network and excess neuronal energy to motor-cortex activity and laughter. Practical realization required extensive databases, and the first dedicated conference followed in 1996.

explainer.example: A pun first leads a listener toward one interpretation, then reveals that this reading is false and forces a quick switch. Under Suslov's model, deleting the false reading corresponds to zeroing part of a neural network; the resulting excess neuronal energy is proposed to reach the motor cortex and contribute to laughter.

explainer.intuition: A joke can make an interpretation briefly seem plausible before revealing that it is false. In Suslov's account, the speed with which that false version leaves consciousness helps create the humorous effect, so timing matters alongside ambiguity.
howItWorks: Process information that permits more than one interpretation.
Form a version that subsequently proves false.
Detect the error and quickly delete that version from consciousness.
Associate the rapid correction, together with ambiguity and timing, with a humorous effect.
In the proposed neural model, zero part of the network and direct excess neuronal energy toward the motor cortex, producing muscular contractions associated with laughter.
explainer.whyItMatters: It offers a computational way to connect linguistic ambiguity, timing, consciousness, and laughter. It also shows why a theory alone was not enough: practical implementation depended on extensive databases that were not initially available.
misconceptions: It is not simply joke-writing; it is computer-based research into humor.
Ambiguity alone is not the whole proposal: the timing of deleting a false interpretation is also essential.
The neural-network account was not a fully realized practical system, partly because it required extensive databases.
